title: Car Rental System
summary: A date-range availability and pricing case study: reserving by category vs by vehicle, and checking interval overlap efficiently across a fleet.

slides.markdown:
Designing a car rental system (Zipcar/Hertz-style) shifts the interview's center of gravity away
from a single-transaction state machine — there's no "one customer, one session" here — and onto
**date-range availability**: can this category of vehicle be reserved for these five days, checked
efficiently across a whole fleet, not just "is this one car free right now."

Get `Vehicle`, `VehicleCategory`, `Reservation`, and `Branch` sketched fast, then spend your time
on the interval-overlap check and the pricing strategy — those are what separate a working answer
from a strong one.

Scope it as: a **catalog** of vehicles grouped into **categories** (economy, SUV, luxury),
customers make **reservations** for a date range, vehicles get **picked up** and **returned** at a
branch, and a **fee** is computed from duration, category, and any late or damage charges.

Non-goal: route optimization — which branch should stock which vehicles, fleet rebalancing — that's
a logistics-optimization problem, worth naming and setting aside so the round stays focused on the
reservation and availability model.

slides.sectionTitle: Core entities: Vehicle, VehicleCategory, Reservation, Branch, RentalAgreement
slides.markdown:
`Vehicle` (VIN, category, current branch), `VehicleCategory` (economy/SUV/luxury, its own rate),
`Reservation` (customer, category or specific vehicle, date range, status), `Branch` (a physical
location holding a subset of the fleet), and `RentalAgreement` (the finalized contract created at
pickup, distinct from the `Reservation` that preceded it).

Keeping `Reservation` and `RentalAgreement` separate is worth stating out loud: a reservation is a
promise about the future; an agreement is what actually happened once a specific vehicle changed
hands — conflating them makes "the reserved category had no cars left at pickup" awkward to model.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: class diagram for vehicles, categories, reservations
slides.markdown:
![Branch, Vehicle, Reservation, and RentalAgreement relationships](assets/car-rental-class-diagram.svg)

`Reservation` points at a `VehicleCategory` by default and only at a specific `Vehicle` once one
is actually assigned — the diagram keeps that association optional on purpose, matching the
reserve-type-then-assign-at-pickup model most large rental chains actually use.

assets.alt: Branch, Vehicle, Reservation, and RentalAgreement relationships

slides.sectionTitle: The hard part: checking date-range overlap efficiently
slides.markdown:
The naive approach — a per-day boolean grid, `isBooked[vehicleId][date]` — works, but wastes
memory proportional to fleet size times the booking horizon in days, and checking a 5-day range
means checking 5 separate booleans per vehicle.

The better structure: keep each vehicle's bookings as a sorted set of non-overlapping date
intervals. Checking whether a new range overlaps existing bookings becomes a small number of
interval comparisons for that vehicle — not one check per day in the range. This is the same shape
of problem as calendar double-booking detection.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: an interval-overlap check for two candidate reservations
slides.markdown:
![Timeline showing an overlapping booking window](assets/booking-overlap-timeline.svg)

Two ranges overlap exactly when `existing.start < candidate.end && candidate.start < existing.end`
— a two-comparison check per existing booking, not a day-by-day scan. Getting the strict-vs-inclusive
boundary right (does a checkout on day 7 conflict with a pickup on day 7?) is the detail
interviewers probe for here.

assets.alt: Timeline showing an overlapping booking window

slides.sectionTitle: Pricing as a strategy: duration, category, late/damage fees
slides.markdown:
Total price composes from independent pieces: a base **duration rate** (per-day or per-week,
often with a multi-day discount curve), a **category multiplier** (an SUV costs more per day than
an economy car), and post-return **fees** — late return, damage, cleaning — applied after the
agreement closes.

Model each as its own component a `PricingStrategy` combines, rather than one formula with every
case baked in — adding a new fee type, a one-way drop fee say, means adding a component, not
editing a monolithic price calculation every other fee type also depends on.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: lock a specific vehicle at booking vs lock only a category
slides.markdown:
| | Lock specific vehicle at booking | Lock only category, assign at pickup |
|---|---|---|
| What the customer sees | a confirmed VIN at booking time | "you have an SUV" confirmed at booking |
| Fleet flexibility | that exact vehicle is unavailable to everyone else, even if a near-identical one frees up | any vehicle in the category works, including one returned or transferred in |
| Operational risk | that specific vehicle breaks down or is delayed returning — no easy substitute | any available vehicle in the category covers it |
| Best fit | premium/exact-model bookings where the customer chose a specific car | standard fleet rental (economy, SUV, etc.) |

**How to decide:** most large rental chains lock only the category for exactly this reason — a
specific-vehicle lock turns one delayed return into a broken promise, while a category lock
absorbs it.

slides.sectionTitle: Extending to one-way rentals (pickup branch A, return branch B)
slides.markdown:
A one-way rental means a vehicle reserved at branch A is expected back at branch B — the
availability check now has to account for a vehicle becoming unavailable at its *origin* branch
for new local reservations once it's committed to leaving, and becoming newly available at the
*destination* branch once it arrives.

I'd model this by having `Vehicle.currentBranch` update on drop-off, not on pickup, and having
`Branch.reserve` only consider vehicles whose committed location — accounting for any in-progress
one-way trips — will actually be at that branch during the requested range. That's really the
interval-overlap check from earlier, applied per-branch instead of assuming a vehicle never
leaves.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: computing availability by scanning every reservation
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "To check if a vehicle is free for a date range, loop through all its
`Reservation` records and check each one for overlap."

**Why it's wrong:** it works for a handful of bookings per vehicle and degrades as a popular
vehicle or category accumulates a full season's worth of reservations — every availability check
re-scans a growing list instead of using a structure built for exactly this query.

**Correct model:** maintain the sorted, non-overlapping interval structure per vehicle (or per
category) as the source of truth, updated on every reservation and cancellation — availability is
answered by a small number of interval comparisons, not a scan of history.
